title: Limits & continuity
examples: When does a function stop being continuous?
How do I use the limit notation correctly?
What is the difference between a limit and the function value?

explain.say: Today we will learn about limits and continuity in functions. Limits tell us what a function approaches. We look at the value as x gets very close to a point. This does not mean the function has to equal that value.

items: Limits show what a function approaches.
We check the value as x nears a point.
The function doesn't need to equal that value.

explain.say: The notation lim x approaches a of f x means we evaluate the limit. We are finding the value that f x approaches as x gets close to a. For example, we might look at lim x approaches 2 of x squared minus 1.

One-sided limits check the approach from one direction only. We use lim x approaches a from the left for approaching from smaller numbers. We use lim x approaches a from the right for approaching from larger numbers.

A function is continuous if it has no breaks or jumps at a point. Three conditions must be met for continuity at a point a. First, f of a must exist. Second, the limit must exist. Third, they must both equal each other.

faq.q: What does it mean for a limit to exist?
faq.a: It means the function approaches the same single value from both sides. If it approaches different values, the limit does not exist. You might ask: Does the limit have to be a number? Or: When is the limit undefined?
asks: Does the limit have to be a number?

faq.q: If the function is not defined at a point, can the limit still exist?
faq.a: Yes, the limit can exist even if the function is not defined there. We are only concerned with the approach, not the actual point. You might ask: Can the limit exist with a hole in the graph? Or: Does the function value matter for the limit?
asks: Can the limit exist with a hole in the graph?
Does the function value matter for the limit?

faq.q: How do I check for continuity in a piecewise function?
faq.a: You must check the limit from the left and the right at the joining point. Then you must check if the function value matches that limit. You might ask: What if the pieces don't meet? Or: Do I check every point?
asks: What if the pieces don't meet?

faq.q: What is the difference between a limit and the function value?
faq.a: The limit is the intended height as we get close. The function value is the actual height at that exact spot. They are not always the same thing. You might ask: Is the limit always equal to f(a)? Or: What if the graph jumps?
asks: Is the limit always equal to f(a)?

faq.q: When do I use one-sided limits?
faq.a: You use them when the function behaves differently approaching from the left versus the right. This often happens at vertical asymptotes or jump discontinuities. You might ask: When is the left limit different from the right limit? Or: What is a jump discontinuity?
asks: When is the left limit different from the right limit?

facts: The limit describes the value a function approaches, not necessarily the value it equals.
For a function to be continuous at point a, the limit as x approaches a must equal f(a).
The left-hand limit and the right-hand limit must both exist and be equal for the overall limit to exist.
A removable discontinuity occurs when the limit exists but the function value is undefined or different.

quiz.say: Evaluate lim x approaches 3 of x squared plus 5.
quiz.why: We substitute 3 into the function, giving 3 squared plus 5, which equals 14.

wrong.0: This only considers the x value, ignoring the function.
wrong.1: This confuses the limit with the value of x.
wrong.3: This is the calculation, not the final answer.

quiz.say: If lim x approaches 1 from the left is 4 and lim x approaches 1 from the right is 6, what is lim x approaches 1 of f(x)?
quiz.why: Because the left and right limits are not equal, the overall limit does not exist.

wrong.1: This incorrectly averages the two different limits.
wrong.2: This only considers the limit from the left side.
wrong.3: This only considers the limit from the right side.

quiz.say: For f(x) to be continuous at x equals 4, what must be true?

options.show: The limit must equal the function value.
options.say: The limit must equal the function value.

options.show: The left and right limits must match.
options.say: The left and right limits must match.

quiz.why: Continuity requires the limit approaching the point to match the actual value at the point.

wrong.0: Continuity applies to many types of functions, not just straight lines.
wrong.2: While necessary, this is only one of the three conditions.
wrong.3: This is only checking if the limit exists, not if it matches f(4).
